Optimization

Source: vignettes/optimization.Rmd
optimization.Rmd

Overview

The tool leverages systematic conservation planning techniques to identify priority areas for conservation, tourism, and scientific management (Giakoumi et al., 2025). Here we provide a description of mathematical optimization problem that underpins the tool. Broadly speaking, the optimization problem is formulated as a multi-objective mixed integer programming problem (Rodrigues et al., 2000). This means that it can be readily be solved using commercial or open source exact algorithm solvers, such as Gurobi or HiGHS (Gurobi Optimization LLC, 2026; Huangfu & Hall, 2017).

Problem formulation

To begin with, we will define the following terminology. Let Z (indexed by z) denote the set of management zones. In particular, the management zones represent the range of potential management options that are available. For convenience, here we let z=c denote the conservation zone, z=s the scientific zone, and z=t the tourism zone. Also let I (indexed by i) denote the set of features considered for management. Although features often pertain to biodiversity elements (e.g., species, ecosystems), here we consider additional features that may also be relevant to scientific and tourism areas (e.g., geological sites, points of interest for tourism, existing scientific infrastructure). Additionally, let J (indexed by j) denote the set of planning units (e.g., areas available for management). Broadly speaking, the tool aims to help inform which planning units j \in J should be allocated to zones z \in Z.

We define terminology to describe the spatial distribution of the features and stakeholder preferences for their representation. In particular, let A_{ij} indicate the amount of each feature i \in I (e.g., abundance of penguins, hectares of lichen, presence/absence of geological sites) that is present within each planning unit j \in J. Representation targets are used to specify the minimum amount of each feature that should ideally be held (covered) by planning units allocated to a particular zone (e.g., total abundance of penguins required in conservation areas, total abundance of penguins required in tourism areas, total hectares of lichen present in conservation areas, total number of geological sites for scientific areas). To quantify such targets, let R_{iz} denote the representation target for feature i \in I by management zone z \in Z. Additionally, to quantify the relative importance for meeting a particular representation target, let W_{iz} denote a positive weight value for each feature i \in I and management zone z \in Z.

We define terminology to describe the location of existing management zones that cannot be altered. For example, it would be impractical to decommission infrastructure in existing scientific areas, or de-gazette existing protected areas (i.e., Antarctic Specially Protected Areas). To describe this, let L_{jz} indicate if planning unit j \in J is currently allocated to zone z \in Z and must remain allocated to this zone during optimization. In other words, these L_{jz} variables will subsequently be used to “lock” planning units to a particular zone.

We define terminology to describe the negative impacts associated with implementing management zones. To describe the foregone economic opportunity associated with establishing conservation and scientific areas, let n_j denote the opportunity cost for planning j. Since detailed site-level revenue data are not readily available across the entire Antarctic Peninsula, we parameterized n_j based on the average number of tourists that have visited planning unit j over a predefined period of time as a proxy. Additionally, let q_j denote the level of impact that tourism operations have on local biodiversity present in planning unit j. Because the population viability analyses required to parameterize species-specific responses to tourism operations are not readily available for all species in the Antarctic Peninsula, we parameterized q_j based on the irreplaceability of the conservation features present in planning unit j (eqn 1) (i.e,. measured according to rarity-weighted richness; Williams et al., 1996). Thus we assume that planning units containing a greater number of species with localized distributions would be more negatively impacted by tourism impacts.

q_j = \sum_{j \in J} \begin{cases} \tag{eqn 1} \frac{\big( \frac{A_{ij}}{max_{i \in I} A_{ij}} \big)}{\sum_{i \in I} A_{ij}}, \text{if $R_{j,z=c} > 0$} \\\\ 0, \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

We define the binary X_{iz} decision variables (eqn 2). Briefly, these variables represent the primary uncertainty in the decision making process. For a given solution, the X_{iz} variables indicate which planning units are allocated to each zone.

X_{iz} = \begin{cases} \tag{eqn 2} 1, \text{if planning unit $i$ selected for zone $z$} \\\\ 0, \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

We define the continuous S_{iz} auxiliary variables (eqn 3). Briefly, these variables represent calculations based on the decision variables. For a given solution, the S_{iz} variables describes the percentage of the target for feature i \in I and zone z \in Z that remains unfulfilled by the solution (in other words, relative target shortfall). In other words, these variables describe how poorly the solution meets a given target.

S_{iz} = \text{relative target shortfall for feature $i$ by zone $z$} \tag{eqn 3}

We define the continuous \alpha_c, \alpha_s, \alpha_t, \beta, \gamma objective variables (eqn 4a–4e). Briefly, these variables represent the performance metrics that are maximized or minimized during optimization. For a given solution, the \alpha_c, \alpha_s, and \alpha_t variables measure the weighted sum of the relative target shortfalls for the conservation, scientific, and tourism zones (respectively). Additionally, the \beta variable measures the total opportunity costs associated with the planning units allocated to the conservation and scientific zones. Furthermore, the \gamma variable measures the total impacts of tourism areas on biodiversity.

\begin{align*} \alpha_{c} &= \text{overall representation target shortfalls for conservation areas ($z=c$)} \tag{eqn 4a} \\ \alpha_{s} &= \text{overall representation target shortfalls for scientific areas ($z=s$)} \tag{eqn 4b} \\ \alpha_{t} &= \text{overall representation target shortfalls for tourism areas ($z=t$)} \tag{eqn 4c} \\ \beta &= \text{total opportunity cost of conservation and scientific areas} \tag{eqn 4d} \\ \gamma &= \text{total impacts of tourism areas on biodiversity} \tag{eqn 4e} \end{align*}

Based on the previous defined terminology, the optimization problem is formulated as the following multi-objective mixed integer programming problem (eqns 5a–5k).

\begin{align*} \text{Minimize } & \alpha_c, \alpha_s, \alpha_t, \beta, \gamma & \tag{eqn 5a} \\ \text{Subject to } & \alpha_c = \sum_{i \in I} W_{i,z=c} \times \frac{S_{i,z=c}}{R_{i,z=c}} & \tag{eqn 5b} \\ & \alpha_s = \sum_{i \in I} W_{i,z=s} \times \frac{S_{i,z=s}}{R_{i,z=s}} & \tag{eqn 5c} \\ & \alpha_t = \sum_{i \in I} W_{i,z=t} \times \frac{S_{i,z=t}}{R_{i,z=t}} & \tag{eqn 5d} \\ & \beta = \big( \sum_{j \in J} n_j \times X_{j,z=t} \big) + \big( \sum_{j \in J} n_j \times X_{j,z=t} \big) & \tag{eqn 5e} \\ & \gamma = \sum_{j \in J} q_j \times X_{j,z=t} & \tag{eqn 5f} \\ & \big( \sum_{j \in J} A_{ij} \big) + \big( R_{iz} \times S_{iz} \big) \geq R_{iz} & \forall i \in i, z \in Z \tag{eqn 5g} \\ & X_{jz} \geq L_{jz} & \forall j \in J, z \in Z \tag{eqn 5h} \\ & \sum_{z \in Z} X_{jz} \leq 1 & \forall j \in J \tag{eqn 5i} \\ & X_{jz} \in \{0, 1\} & \forall j \in J, z \in Z \tag{eqn 5j} \\ & S_{iz} \in [0, 1] & \forall i \in i, z \in Z \tag{eqn 5k} \\ \end{align*}

Here (eqn 5a) objectives are defined to minimize overall representation target shortfalls for (i) conservation areas, (ii) scientific areas, and (iii) tourism areas, as well as minimize (iv) total opportunity cost associated with conservation and scientific areas and (v) total impact of tourism areas on biodiversity (refer to the following section for details on how these objectives are optimized). Constraints (eqn 5b–5d) specify that the total representation target shortfall variables (i.e., \alpha_{c}, \alpha_{s}, \alpha_{t}) are calculated as the weighted sum of the relative target shortfall variables (per S_{iz}) associated with each zone. Constraint (eqn 5e) ensures that the total opportunity cost associated with conservation and scientific areas variable (i.e., \beta) is calculated based on the opportunity costs associated with planning units allocated to the conservation and scientific zones. In a similar manner, constraint (eqn 5f) ensures that the total impact of tourism areas variable (i.e., \gamma) is calculated based on the level of impact that tourism would have on planning units allocated to the tourism zone. Constraints (eqn 5g) express the relative target shortfall variables (i.e., S_{iz}) is calculated as the proportion of each target that remains remains unfulfilled (similar to Jung et al., 2021). Constraints (eqn 5h) ensure that the existing management areas (per L_{jz}) are locked (in other words, cannot be altered) during optimization. Constraints (eqn 5i) ensure that each planning unit can only be allocated to, at most, a single zone. Finally, constraints specify that the (eqn 5j) decision variables are binary and (eqn 5k) auxiliary variable are continuous and bounded between zero and one.

Multi-objective optimization approach

The tool employs the reference point approach to accommodate multiple objectives (López Jaimes et al., 2011; Wierzbicki, 1980). Briefly, this approach uses parameters to specify aspirational levels of performance for each objective (hereafter, reference points) and as well as parameters to specify the relative importance for achieving the reference point for each objective (hereafter, weight parameters). Additionally, this approach can be augmented with scaling factors to ensure that differences in scale among the objectives do not bias the optimization process (following Deléglise et al., 2024). In particular, these scaling factors are calculated based on the performance of the best possible solution (hereafter, utopian points) and worst possible solution (hereafter, dystopian points) for each objective (separately). Indeed, the scaling factors are critical for ensuring that the weight parameters accurately reflect user preferences during optimization (Das & Dennis, 1997).

Here we define additional terminology to describe the multi-objective optimization approach. Let O (indexed by o) denote the set of objectives and v_o denote the previously defined objective variables (i.e., v = \{ \alpha_c, \alpha_s, \alpha_t, \beta, \gamma \}. Also let r_o denote the reference point parameter, w_o the weight parameter for each objective o \in O, and s_o denote the scaling factor each objective o \in O. To calculate the scaling factors (eqn 6a), let u_o and d_o denote the utopian and dystopian points for each objective o \in O. These utopian and dystopian points, in turn, are precomputed by solving the optimization problems for each objective (separately) (eqns 6b and 6c).

\begin{align*} s_o &= \frac{1}{\| u_o - d_o \|} & \tag{eqn 6a} \\ u_o &= \min(V_o), & \text{subject to (eqns 5b--5k)} \tag{eqn 6b} \\ d_o &= \max(V_o), & \text{subject to (eqns 5b--5k)} \tag{eqn 6c} \\ \end{align*}

We define the continuous \lambda_{o} auxiliary variables (eqn 7). Same as before, these variables represent calculations based on the decision variables. For a given solution, the \lambda_{o} variables describe the (weighted and normalized) shortfall in performance for how well the solution achieves each objective o \in O. For example, a larger value means that the solution has poorer performance and a smaller value means better performance according to a particular objective (relative to the weight parameter and scaling factor for that objective, per w_o and s_o).

\lambda_{o} = \text{performance shortfall for objective $o$} \tag{eqn 7}

Given the previously defined terminology, the tool uses the following multi-objective optimization approach to accommodate multiple objectives (eqn 8).

\begin{align*} \text{Lexicographic minimize } & \max_{o \in O} \lambda_o, \sum_{o \in O} \lambda_o & \tag{eqn 8a} \\ \text{Subject to } & \lambda_o = w_o \times s_o \times (v_o - r_o) & \forall o \in O \tag{eqn 8b} \\ & \text{(eqns 5b--5k)} & \\ \end{align*}

Here (eqn 8a) the multi-objective optimization approach involves minimizing the largest performance shortfall variables among all objectives and, subsequently, minimizing the sum of the performance shortfall variables. This is an important component of the reference point method because it will help ensure that solutions achieve, at least, a moderate level of performance across each and every multiple objective—rather than severely sacrificing some objectives to achieve an especially high level of performance for other objectives. Although this component is typically expressed using a weighted sum, the tool leverages lexicographic optimization techniques instead to avoid numerical instability issues associated with tiny values that can degrade solver performance (Klotz & Newman, 2013; López Jaimes et al., 2011). Constraint (eqn 8b) specifies that the performance shortfall variable for a given objective (i.e., \lambda_o) is calculated based on the weight parameter (per w_o), scaling factor (s_o), and difference between the reference point parameter (per r_o) and the objective value (per v_o) for that objective. Constraints (5b–5k) ensure that the objective values (i.e., v_o) are calculated correctly.

Tool parameters

The tool aims to provide a flexible and user-friendly interface for identifying priority areas and navigating trade-offs. Although the problem formulation and multi-objective optimization approach involve a large number of terms, many of these terms are parameterized based on underlying data (e.g., A_{ij} and L_{jz} are based on data from Lee et al., 2024) or can be precomputed automatically based on preliminary analyses (e.g., u_o and d_o). To provide a positive user experience that will facilitate trade-off exploration, the tool has parameters for specifying terms that reflect stakeholder preferences. In particular, the tool has parameters for the (R_{iz}) percentage of each feature i \in I that should be represented by areas allocated to zone z, (W_{iz}) relative importance for representing each feature i \in I by areas allocated to zone z, and (w_o) relative importance for achieving each objective o \in O. Note that the reference points (r_o) will be set based on the precomputed utopian points (u_o) to reduce tool complexity. Additionally, since there are too many features and zones for users to set parameters for each feature and zone individually, the features are grouped together based on common themes (e.g., penguins, seabirds, habitat types, invertebrates, plants and mosses) and parameters can be used to alter representation target and weight values for entire groups of features. Note that these feature groups will be identified in consultation with experts and stakeholders. Because previous work has already elicited representation target values from stakeholders, the tool will provide options for systematically increasing or decreasing these target values (e.g., increase or decrease targets by 15%, 25%, or 50%).
